flying-robot vision · synthetic validation

Where the pose error actually comes from

A 5-DOF estimator recovers the robot's position and rotor axis by back-projecting the image ellipse of its 20.4 mm duct ring. It is accurate to 0.75 mm — but that number says nothing about which direction the error points, which part of the fit produced it, or how much of it is even removable. These overlays, curves and Cramér–Rao bounds answer all three.

cost of a wrong branch

Depth carries almost all of it. Lateral position is 6× better than depth, and that ratio is geometry, not tuning: lateral comes from the ellipse's centre, depth from its size. Monocular size-ranging uses the object as its own baseline, and this baseline is 20.4 mm wide. The exact penalty is g(θ)·z/(2R) with g(0) = √3 — range over diameter, times a factor between 1.73 and 2.18 that is the price of having to estimate the tilt from the same ellipse. Derived and verified below.

shipped · axial weighting

The rod was being fitted as if it were the rim

The mast and magnet stick out along the rotor axis, so as the robot tilts they push the silhouette outward in its short direction — and because they sit on the axis, they land near the middle of the major axis. Weighting each hull point by how far along that axis it lies, w = |proj|/a, suppresses them. Same pose in each pair, weighting off then on.

An earlier version of this page said the weighting was off because it collapses the certification gate from ~13% of frames to ~1–3.5%. That claim is withdrawn. It was measured while PoseEstimator.update forced the weighted fit regardless of the flag, so both arms ran weighted; the two figures came from unrelated runs and a third from a different metric entirely. The pairs below were byte-identical for the same reason, and are now genuinely different.

The controlled A/B — same seed, same 400 poses, same gate, same constants, the flag the only difference:

640×4802.0%2.0%0.338 mm 0.296 mm0.371°0.244°

Certified frames over the six usable modes: 61 off, 59 on — the same. Modes at 100% in spec: 5/8 off, 6/8 on. The weighting costs no gate coverage and improves both metrics in every mode, so it is now on — the pairs below describe the shipped build.

The matched-set objection that kept it off was also wrong. The claim was that the weighted fit needs RADIUS_MM = 10.2662 against the unweighted 10.2446; refitting the radius from a dataset regenerated with the weighting on gives 10.2418 — 0.03% away, an order of magnitude inside the residual it was supposed to bias. The two fits do not need different radii.

Regenerating the whole chain for the weighted fit was tried and rejected on measurement, which is worth recording because it is the opposite of what "make it self-consistent" predicts:

configurationcertified frames (6 usable core modes) modes at 100% in spec
axial off, original constants615/8
axial on, original constants (shipped) 596/8
axial on, fully refit constants127/8

The refit trades 59 certified frames for 12 to gain one mode, and the refitted error model looks unhealthy — its own held-out acceptance fell from 3.5% to 0.9%, and its fitted log_inv_margin coefficient went negative (−1.6, from +1.03). A sign flip on a feature meaning “how far apart the two ambiguity branches were” is not a physically sensible model. Refitting it properly is open work; that coefficient is the lead.

final evaluation · per sensor mode

Does it meet ±1° and ±0.5 mm on every frame it reports?

Stereo-fused, 400 poses, with the certification gate. The contract is not the median — it is the worst frame among those the estimator agrees to report. Declining a frame it cannot certify is correct behaviour, so detection rate sits beside every accuracy figure; without it, “100% in spec” is trivially achievable by reporting nothing.

Read the detection column, not the in-spec column. The gate is doing its job — every frame it certifies is in specification — but it certifies only a few percent of frames, and that number is currently understated. The error model it uses was fitted through the estimator while a default-argument bug forced the axial-weighted fit, which is what now ships — so the gate and the fit do at least match. But every configuration tried certifies ~3% at 1280×800 where an earlier sweep certified 13% on 800 poses, and that gap is identical across the axial A/B, so it is drift elsewhere in the chain and is not diagnosed. Read this as a lower bound on achievable coverage.

the information floor · what no estimator can beat

How much of the error is even removable?

A residual is uninterpretable without a floor to compare it against: a millimetre could mean the solver is sloppy, or it could mean the information is not in the image, and those point at opposite work. The Cramér–Rao bound settles it. Derivations in bounds.py, 60+ Monte-Carlo checks in test_bounds.py, this comparison from limits.py (391 frames spanning tilt 0–70° and both condition tiers, so the “measured” row below is harder than the headline band at the top of this page and the two are not directly comparable).

The solver is already at the bound. End-to-end Monte Carlo — noisy boundary points through the shipped ellipse fit and the shipped back-projection — gives statistical efficiencies of 0.94–1.06 on every pose component, and 0.96–1.01 on the five ellipse parameters. The direct algebraic fit is famously biased toward small ellipses and the reflex is to replace it with an iterative maximum-likelihood fit; at this noise level there is nothing to recover. Whatever explains the gap below, it is not the solver.

levelstatus‖position‖ mm depth mmlateral mmangle °

+ convex hullbound0.49020.48820.03580.249
noise-equivalentprediction2.35812.34440.20001.374
measuredmeasured1.81951.78420.24742.668

The first three are bounds — nothing may beat them. The fourth is a prediction: what independent Gaussian boundary error of the measured size would produce. The estimator beats it, and that is itself the finding — real boundary errors are correlated, and their common mode is exactly what the radius calibration absorbs. Pose error is scored against the oracle ambiguity branch, because a local bound cannot describe a likelihood with two equal maxima.

The depth law, corrected

Every earlier section here quotes z/(2R). That is the tilt-known case. Estimating tilt from the same ellipse costs a further √3, because the semi-axis must be disentangled from the minor axis and the rotation — the (a,b) Fisher block is (N/8σ²)[[3,1],[1,3]], giving σa = √3 σ/√N.

tilt0°10°30°60°80°
g(θ)1.7321.7401.8112.0382.180

At 250 mm and 30° the depth penalty is 22.2× lateral, not the 12.3× the naive form gives. Noise level, point count, focal length and resolution all cancel — verified invariant to 0.4% across 16 combinations, and to six significant figures between N = 500 and 8000. A practical form is σdepth ≈ (z/R) σlateral, range over radius, good to 15% at any tilt.

The 71×, factored

The three bounds multiply out as 6.0 × 3.2 × 3.7 = 71. It is tempting to read that as three budgets to attack. Only one is fully open.

stepfactorrecoverable?
photon → pixel-quantised6.0× No — and not for the obvious reason
quantised → hulled3.2× Yes — untouched, this is the lever
hulled → measured3.7× Partly — see below

Why the first is not recoverable. Sub-pixel refinement does beat quantisation — subpixel_boundary reaches 0.076 px on a clean disc against an edge bound of 0.052 px, a 3.8× gain over the 0.289 px quantisation floor. It buys nothing here because the traced curve sits 1.087 px from the rim whether it is located to 0.289 px or 0.076 px. That is the derived form of the earlier measured result: an 18× improvement in edge localisation bought 2% of the outcome.

Why the second is. The convex hull keeps 31 vertices of a ~354 px perimeter, and 1/√N is not negotiable but N is. The hull is there to enforce the outward-only property the one-sided loss depends on — on real captures 42–62% of dense contour points lie inside the fitted ellipse — so the version that survives is dense contour points restricted to the hull.

Why the third is only partly open. What remains is that the silhouette is not the rim: the rod and magnet project into the outline, and which non-circular shape is presented changes frame to frame. Mostly that needs a fiducial on the rim, illumination that lights only the rim, or a forward model that separates rim from mast. But the axial weighting already recovered some of it in software, by modelling where the contamination is rather than fitting harder to the contaminated boundary — which is why it works where trimming by residual did not.

Sub-pixel refinement, against its own bound

Synthetic soft-edged disc of known radius, C=200, σn=5, PSF 1.2 px. The refinement works; it is not what is limiting.

biasscatter
thresholded contour−0.461 px0.269 px
after refinement−0.038 px0.076 px
edge Cramér–Rao bound—0.052 px
measured on real renders+0.857 px1.087 px

At most 1.46× remains in edge localisation, ever, by any method — acting on a term that is already 14× below the one that matters. A perfect sensor moves the total by under 5%.

Two things no engineering removes. Rolling the rim about its own axis maps the circle onto itself, so the image derivative with respect to roll is zero — measured at 1.6×10−12 px over 64 roll angles. And a quadric cone admits exactly two circular cross-sections, so two poses whose normals differ by 49° reproject to ellipses that agree to 4.2×10−12 px. The single-view likelihood has two exactly equal maxima; prior-free branch selection is wrong on 48% of independent frames, which is the size of the problem the temporal prior and the second camera exist to solve — not a shipped failure rate.

failure modes

The frames that go wrong, and why

About 1% of frames under realistic noise fail badly. They are not scattered randomly — every one sits in a corner of the condition space that can be named, and you can see the cause: the fitted ellipse lands on the blade cross instead of the rim.

conditions

What the estimator sees as things get harder

Tilt, lighting, background and opacity. Opacity and background barely move the result until background reaches the threshold itself; tilt and ambient light are what matter.

All figures are synthetic: the robot mesh rendered through the rig's measured intrinsics, so ground truth is exact. Numbers come from a held-out split the calibration never saw. Orientation is scored against the better of the two back-projection branches — a single view of a circle cannot tell them apart, which is what the ambiguity figure above costs when the choice goes wrong. Resolving it needs a second camera.
